title: Grammar Terms: Voice and Punctuation
keyIdea: Year 6 writers use exact terms. The subject is who or what a sentence is about; the object receives the action of the verb. In the active voice the subject does the action; in the passive voice the subject has the action done to it. Synonyms mean the same, antonyms mean the opposite. A hyphen joins words into one, a colon introduces a list or an explanation, a semi-colon joins two linked full sentences, an ellipsis shows a pause or missing words, and bullet points set out a list down the page.

kid: Every sentence has a subject. It is who or what the sentence is about, and it usually comes before the verb. In Priya painted a tiger, Priya is the subject. The tiger is the object, because it receives the action.

Not every verb takes an object. In The baby slept all night, nothing gets slept, so there is no object. In a passive sentence, like The window was broken by the ball, the window is the subject even though the ball did the breaking.
A synonym means the same as another word, like huge and enormous. An antonym means the opposite, like ancient and modern. Knowing both helps you pick the exact word you need.

Punctuation marks have jobs. A hyphen joins two words into one, as in man-eating shark. A colon points ahead to a list or a reason. A semi-colon joins two full sentences that belong together. An ellipsis, three dots, shows a pause or words left out. Bullet points split a list into lines.
adult: The English national curriculum lists these terms in the Year 6 grammar appendix: subject, object, active, passive, synonym, antonym, ellipsis, hyphen, colon, semi-colon and bullet points. Pupils are expected to use the terms when they talk about their own writing, not just recognise them on a worksheet.

The subject is defined by its place and its link to the verb, not by who does the action. In a passive clause the subject is the receiver, the verb is a form of be plus a past participle, and the doer can appear in a by-phrase. Intransitive verbs such as slept, arrived or laughed take no object at all.

Common mistakes: calling the doer the subject in every sentence, so The cake was eaten by Max gets Max as subject. Treating any noun after the verb as an object, such as all night. Joining two full sentences with a comma (a comma splice). Putting a semi-colon before a list, or a colon between two equal sentences. Using an ellipsis as a full stop with extra dots.

In the lab, learners tap the subject and object of four sentences, including one with no object and one in the passive. They decide where a hyphen changes meaning, choose a colon, semi-colon or comma between clauses, and match the ellipsis, bullet points and hyphen to their jobs. The challenge adds synonyms, antonyms and active versus passive.

familyTip: Pick a sentence from a reading book and take turns naming its subject and object. Then hunt for one colon, semi-colon, hyphen or ellipsis on the page and say what job it is doing there.

visual.caption: Colon or semi-colon? Drag each sentence to the mark it needs, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Bring three things _ a pen, a ruler and a rubber.
It was late _ the shops had shut.
She had one goal _ to win the cup.
Tom likes maths _ Ana prefers art.
You will need _ flour, eggs and butter.
The bell rang _ everyone ran outside.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: tap subjects and objects, use a hyphen to change meaning, choose a colon or semi-colon, then match each mark to its job.

practice.prompt: In The letter was posted by Kai, what is the subject?
practice.hint: The subject comes before the verb, even when it is not the doer.
practice.explain: The sentence is passive, so the letter is the subject and Kai, the doer, sits in the by-phrase. Posted is part of the verb.

practice.prompt: A paragraph has {a} sentences joined with a semi-colon and {b} sentences that end with an ellipsis. Each semi-colon joins exactly two full sentences. How many full sentences sit either side of the semi-colons?
practice.hint: A semi-colon always has one full sentence before it and one after it.
practice.explain: Each of the {a} semi-colons links two full sentences, so 2 × {a} = {=2*a}. The {b} ellipses do not join anything.

practice.prompt: Which sentence uses a colon correctly?
choices: We packed three things: a tent, a torch and a map.
We packed: three things, a tent.
The tent was up: and we ate.
practice.hint: A colon comes after a complete clause and points ahead to a list or explanation.
practice.explain: We packed three things is complete on its own, and the colon introduces the list. The other colons split a sentence in the wrong place.

practice.prompt: Leo writes {n} sentences. {k} of them use a verb with no object, like slept. How many of his sentences have an object?
practice.hint: Take away the sentences whose verb has no object.
practice.explain: {n} sentences minus the {k} with no object leaves {=n-k} sentences with an object.

pool.prompt: What is the object in The chef chopped the onions?
pool.hint: The object comes after the verb and receives the action.
pool.explain: The onions receive the chopping, so they are the object. The chef is the subject and chopped is the verb.

pool.prompt: Which word is an antonym of generous?
pool.hint: An antonym means the opposite, not the same.
pool.explain: Mean is the opposite of generous. Kind and giving are close in meaning, so they are synonyms.

pool.prompt: Which sentence is in the passive voice?
choices: The match was won by our team.
pool.hint: Look for be plus a past participle with the receiver as subject.
pool.explain: The match was won is passive: the match is the subject and was won is be plus a past participle. Our team was happy has no action done to it.

choices: The sun set, the sky turned pink.
The sun set; the sky turned pink.
As the sun set, the sky turned pink.
pool.hint: A comma splice joins two full sentences with only a comma.
pool.explain: The sun set and the sky turned pink are both full sentences, so a comma alone cannot join them. A semi-colon can.

pool.prompt: Why is there a hyphen in a man-eating shark?
choices: It joins man and eating into one describing word
pool.hint: Think about what the shark does and what the man does.
pool.explain: The hyphen makes man-eating one word that describes the shark. Without it, it sounds like a man eating a shark.

pool.hint: Ask who or what received the action. Is there anything?
pool.explain: Arrived takes no object, and late tells you when. Ate the cake and thanked the host both have an object.

pool.prompt: A poster has {a} bullet points in one list and {b} in another. Each bullet point starts one item. How many items are there?
pool.hint: Each bullet point stands for one item, so add the two lists.
pool.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} items, one for each bullet point.

pool.prompt: In a quote, what does an ellipsis like this show: We will … win?
choices: Some words have been left out
pool.hint: Three dots inside a quote mark a gap.
pool.explain: An ellipsis inside a quote shows that words were cut. It does not add emphasis or start a list.

pool.prompt: Mia finds {s} synonyms and {t} antonyms for the word cold. How many more synonyms than antonyms does she find?
pool.hint: Subtract the number of antonyms from the number of synonyms.
pool.explain: {s} − {t} = {=s-t} more synonyms, like chilly and icy, than antonyms, like hot.
